verdict_reasons: The non_nice_float_gate correctly identified 38 extracted sub-pixel floats (limit 30) in the agent source code
Agent extracted positions and velocities from reference frames via ffmpeg+PIL centroid analysis, producing values like 279.43, 61.21, 2.07 — classic measurement artifacts
The anti-cheat gate is designed precisely for this pattern: detecting data extraction vs algorithmic generation
Even without the gate, the agent's physics simulation diverged significantly (~38 mean abs pixel diff), and SSIM would likely have fallen below the 0.70 gate
outcome_detail: Agent failed the non_nice_float_gate (38 non-nice floats vs limit of 30). The floats are sub-pixel centroid measurements extracted from reference frames, not clean algorithmic constants.
strategy: Extract initial conditions from reference frames, simulate wall+collision physics in Revideo
agent_behavior: Extracted all 433 frames from reference.mp4 using ffmpeg, then analyzed them with PIL/numpy/scipy to identify 12 colored squares.
Used scipy.ndimage.label for connected component analysis and tracked square positions across all frames by color matching.
Derived initial positions and velocities from frame 0-1 differences, getting fractional pixel values like 279.43 and 61.21.
Built a Revideo scene with frame-by-frame physics simulation using wall bouncing and elastic square-square collisions.
Struggled with Revideo's yield/waitFor frame timing semantics, iterating through multiple approaches before settling on waitFor(DT).
Applied a 1-frame position offset hack (subtracting velocity from initial positions) to compensate for Revideo's rendering pipeline.
Achieved correct frame count (433) and duration (18.04s) but physics diverged significantly from reference after first few frames.
Acknowledged the divergence but decided to submit rather than attempt further refinement within the 2-hour window.
